I crouch beside her and look at the drawing in the wet. "Then it's the night of the eighteenth, and we do it in order: the copy in the Counting House first, because it's nearest my gallery and I can pull it down off the shelf with my own hands, and then I climb your drain-stair for the ledger itself. Where are the children kept, Tess, and how do we get them out once the books are ash?"

I touch the broken stump of her horn gently. "Until then you stay hooded and you stay dull, and you don't come to the culvert again. I'll hang a red thread on my belt at dusk the day before if the way is clear, and I'll keep Pip fed and talkative so he writes down boredom instead of me."

input.add_to_description: Day 16 night plan: Korvash hits the Counting House copy first, then climbs the drain-stair for the main ledger, on the night of Day 18. Tessa: the children (about a hundred) sleep in the Low Galleries behind the fourth smelter, locked with a single barred gate whose key hangs in the Counting House; a service tunnel from the Low Galleries ends at the culvert Korvash used (grate rusted, can be forced). Signal: Korvash hangs a red thread on his belt at dusk of Day 17 if the way is clear. Tessa stays hooded and away from the culvert until then.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger
time: 15 minutes later: Day 16, 11:28:36 PM

Tessa nods at your order, and you see her filing it away the way Dargan used to. "The copy first. Good. It's closer, and it's the one he'll trust to be safe." She smooths the drawing in the mud and adds two more lines.

"The children are in the Low Galleries, behind the fourth smelter. A hundred, give or take, sleeping in rows. One barred gate. The key hangs on a hook in the Counting House, near the copy." She taps a thin line. "From the Low Galleries a service tunnel runs out to this culvert. The grate at the end is rusted through. Two strong backs can force it. That's how they leave: through the water, in the dark, while the wall watches the fires."

She reaches up, almost shyly, and lets you touch the stump of her broken horn. "Dargan's trick," she says. "Hit a rock at six. Never mind." Then she pulls her hood up and the mender is back. "Red thread on your belt at dusk if the way is clear. I'll watch for it. I won't come back here till then."

She slips into the arch and is gone, so quiet that the water doesn't change its sound. You stay a moment alone in the cold, then climb the cinder slope to the barracks, boots in hand, past the coal sheds, careful of loose coal. Ruk's torch is a small star on the wall, and he doesn't look down.

You slip into your bunk before the dawn bell. Pip is asleep with his cap over his eyes. The greataxe is where you left it, rolled in the blanket. It is past eleven thirty and you have two days to ready the plan: the copy in the Counting House, the key for the Low Galleries, the drain-stair to the ledger-house, and Pip, who writes everything down.

What does Korvash do?

sheet.name: Korvash Emberhide
sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. Invent only original places and people; keep it grounded in the SRD's monsters (hobgoblins, goblins, bugbears, wolves, etc.).

input.add_to_description: Day 16 night plan: strike the night of Day 18 (two nights hence): the Counting House copy first, then the ledger via the drain-stair. Children (about a hundred) are kept in the Low Pens, a barred gallery under the second smelter, opposite Korvash's own post; the pen door has a bar and a padlock, key held by the pen-warden (a hobgoblin called Gresh) who sleeps in the gatehouse. Tessa does not know a way out for them beyond the culvert and sluice, which a child can crawl through but not quickly. Signal: Korvash hangs a red thread on his belt at dusk on Day 17 if the way is clear. Tessa stays hooded and dull, no more culvert visits.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger
time: 40 minutes later: Day 16, 11:53:36 PM

Tessa watches your finger trace her lines in the wet. She nods at the order of it and frowns at the last part.

"The children are in the Low Pens," she says. "A barred gallery under your own smelter, Kor, right under the door you guard. You've been standing over them for two days." That lands hard, and she sees it land. "Bar and padlock. The pen-warden, Gresh, holds the key and sleeps in the gatehouse. As for getting them out..." She spreads her scarred hands. "The culvert, and the sluice. A child can crawl it. A hundred of them, in the dark, past a wall? I don't know. I have not found the answer."

When you touch the stump of her horn she goes still, then leans into your hand for exactly one breath. "Dull and hooded," she says. "A red thread at dusk. Don't be late, and don't let Pip count your yawns." She turns, and the dark takes her into the arch like a goat into the rocks. You hear water, then nothing.

You climb back through the shadow of the coal sheds, past Ruk's wall, which is quiet now, and ease into the barracks near midnight. Pip is a lump under his cap. The blanket you left over the greataxe has not been disturbed. You lie down, and for the first time in fourteen years the weight on your chest is a different weight.

You have two days. The copy, the ledger, a padlock, a key held by Gresh, a hundred children under your own post, and a sluice just wide enough to crawl. You can't solve it all tonight.

It is nearly midnight on the sixteenth. What does Korvash do next?

input.add_to_description: Day 16 night plan: strike the night of Day 18. Order: Counting House copy first (Korvash), then the ledger-house via drain-stair (Tessa unlatches wash-house door at second bell). Children (about a hundred) are held in the Lower Pens, a barred gallery below the second smelter, one door locked with a key the pen-warden carries; a ventilation adit runs from the pens to the east scree beyond the wall (Tessa has scouted it). Signal: Korvash hangs a red thread on his belt at dusk on Day 17 if clear. Tessa stays hooded and dull until then.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger
time: 30 minutes later: Day 16, 11:43:36 PM

Tessa studies the wet-stone map with you, and her finger moves to a new spot. "The children are in the Lower Pens. A barred gallery under your own smelter, Kor. One door, and the pen-warden carries the key. There's an old vent-adit at the back that runs out under the east scree. I crawled it in autumn. It's tight for you, but children will fit." She looks up. "Copy first, then the ledger, then the pens. The warden I can't do anything about."

You touch the broken stump of her horn, gently. She flinches, then leans into it for half a breath. You tell her to stay hooded and dull, and not to come to the culvert again. You'll hang a red thread on your belt at dusk tomorrow if the way is clear, and keep Pip fed and talkative so he writes boredom instead of you.

"Red thread," she says, almost smiling. "Dargan's trick." She rubs out the drawing with her palm, squeezes your wrist once, and is gone into the arch like water into stone.

You wade out and creep back along the sheds. Ruk's mate has fallen asleep on the parapet and Ruk does not look down. You slip into the barracks a little before midnight, ease the greataxe out of the blanket, and lie down. Pip stirs, mutters "nothing, nothing, boring," in his sleep, and is quiet.

You have the night of the eighteenth to plan. The Counting House is by the lower gate, guarded, with a scribe who sleeps in it. You are due at the gallery door at dawn, and nobody knows what you've done.

What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 16 night plan: strike the night of Day 18. Copy in Counting House first, then the ledger via drain-stair. Tessa: the children are held in the Tally-pens, a barred lower gallery behind the third smelter (the 'cold gallery'), about 90 laborers incl. some 40 children, locked with a chain whose key hangs in the Counting House beside the copy; the cold gallery has an old ventilation adit that exits on the east scree beyond the wall. Signal: Korvash wears a red thread on his belt at dusk of Day 17 if the way is clear. Tessa stays hooded and avoids the culvert.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger
time: 15 minutes later: Day 16, 11:28:36 PM

Tessa nods at your plan, and the nod grows into something near a grin. "Copy first. Good. It's closest, and nobody guards paper they think nobody wants."

She rubs out her drawing and draws another. "The children are in the Tally-pens, behind the third smelter. The cold gallery, they call it, because the fire never reaches it. A barred hall, ninety hands in all, and about forty of them children. A chain on the door. The key hangs in the Counting House, on a hook beside the copy." She taps the far end of the line. "There's an old air-adit at the back of the cold gallery. It comes out on the east scree past the wall. The Foreman thinks it's blocked. It isn't. Not all the way."

That settles the rest. The copy and the key together in one room is a gift. You take the book, take the key, burn the one, and the cold gallery opens before the ledger-house is even touched. Then up the drain-stair for the second book, and out the adit with the children, all by the east scree, before the dawn bell.

She lets you touch the broken stump of her horn, which she would not have allowed anyone else to do, and agrees to everything. She will stay hooded and dull, and she will not come to the culvert again. You will wear a red thread on your belt at dusk on the seventeenth if the way is clear. And Pip will be kept fed and talkative, writing down boredom instead of you.

"Kor." She stops at the arch, a small shape in a hood against the dark. "Whatever happens. I'm glad it was you who came."

Then she is gone into the tunnel, up the sluice, and you wade back out into the cold. It is nearly half past eleven. You have time to reach your bunk before the dawn bell, if no one is watching, and two days to prepare.

line:
I whisper back, "The goat that sings is her, Ninna, my sister the mender, so tell the little ones to be ready at her song and keep quiet till then." I ask her to have the smallest ones loosen the chute bolts' nuts if they can reach them, and to cough and moan about me at the dawn count so Hask thinks I'm dying.

Then I lie slack and gray, breathing shallow, waiting for him to come kneel by the chained prisoner the Foreman wants alive. When his hand's at my throat, I'll rage, seize him and take the key ring before he can shout.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 dawn: agreed to pass the word 'be ready when the goat sings'. The grate bolts are outside, so the children cannot loosen them. Korvash's feigned dying failed: Hask, seeing a man whose color and breathing had plainly recovered overnight, did not kneel; he kept his distance and called two guards to stand over Korvash at the dawn count.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ninna

You whisper it to her: the goat that sings is your sister, the mender, and the little ones are to stay quiet and ready until they hear her song. Ninna nods, and the word passes down the rows in mouths and hands, without a sound. She tells you the bolts on the grate are on the outside, so no small fingers can loosen them from in here. That part of your plan is dead.

Then you lie slack and wait, and somewhere in the waiting your body does what it has to. You sleep. You wake at what must be the small hours with the cuff cold on your ankle, and the pain in your side has dulled to an ache. The bandages have held, and you are stronger than you have any right to be: fully rested, your hurts closed over, the rage banked again in your chest like a coal.

That is the trouble. At the dawn bell, a little before six, Hask rises from his stool with the ring of keys and begins the count down the rows, lips moving. When he reaches you, he stops. You are doing your best to look grey and slack, but your breathing is slow and deep, and your scales have the healthy dull shine of a sleeper's. He studies you for a long moment, then does not kneel. He steps back, says one flat word over his shoulder, and two wall-guards come in from the door with drawn swords and take up stations at your head and feet.

"Rested, I think," says Hask, without any expression at all. "The Foreman will want to see how well." He holds the key ring at arm's length, well out of your reach, and the ring jingles.

Your chain gives you perhaps six feet. Hask is nine feet away with the keys. Two guards stand over you, and two more wait at the door. The children watch in silence. It is six in the morning on the nineteenth, with one night left before the move. You have full hit points, Rage 2/2 and your breath again, and no weapon.

input.add_to_description: Day 18 night: Korvash told her the singing goat is his sister the mender. Ninna passed word down the rows; the smallest children will work the chute-grate nuts loose and she will cough and moan about Korvash at the dawn count. Korvash slept through the night chained (long rest ruled valid: undisturbed 8 hours); he is fully recovered but acts near-dead. Day 19 ~6 AM Hask approaches for the count.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ninna

You whisper it to Ninna: the goat that sings is the mender, your sister. She doesn't ask how. She nods once, and the word goes down the rows of straw in breaths and tugged blankets. Then you lie slack and gray, breathing shallow, and the long night closes over you.

Nobody comes. Sleep takes you in spite of the chain, and when you wake, the cold stone has taken the ache out of your bones and left something steady in its place. The bandages are stiff with dried blood. You are whole again: full strength, your rage banked in your chest and your breath ready, though nobody must see it.

The lamp has been trimmed, and dawn is a grey seam under the door. Down the Row you hear the small sounds of children working at something in the dark, a soft grinding of metal at the back and a hushed "shh." Then Hask's stool scrapes. He stands, stretches the stiffness from his back, takes up his ring of keys and a tally-stick, and begins the count, row by row, murmuring numbers.

Ninna starts to cough. Three other children join her, and then a thin voice says, loudly enough to carry, "The big one's not moving. He's gone cold."

You let your head loll and your breath rattle. Hask's steps slow. He reaches the end of the Row, stops at your feet, and looks down at you for a long moment, his flat face unreadable. The Foreman wants you alive; that much is plain in the way he frowns. He bends, keys swinging from his belt-ring, and kneels in the straw beside your chain with one hand reaching for your throat to feel for a pulse. His hand is a hand's breadth away. The nearest guards are at the barred door, thirty feet behind him, with their backs half turned.

It is just past six in the morning. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 18 night: Korvash told her the singing goat is his sister; she passed word down the rows, and the smallest children will work at the chute bolts and fuss over Korvash at the dawn count. Korvash slept and recovered (long rest) chained in the Row. Day 19 dawn: Hask comes to count and kneels by Korvash.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ninna

You tell Ninna in a whisper that the goat who sings is your sister, the mender. She doesn't smile, but she nods, and her small face changes the way a shuttered window changes when a lamp is lit behind it. The word goes down the rows hand to hand, like a bucket line. Nobody speaks, but you hear blankets shift all through the dark.

Then you lie slack and gray and breathe shallow, and somewhere in that you sleep. Chained, bandaged, and watched by ninety children who have decided to be your guard, you sleep eight hours, and nothing wakes you. You come up out of it a little before dawn with your strength back: fourteen hit points, your rage banked, and your breath ready. The bandages on your ribs are dry.

The dawn bell tolls. Hask rises from his stool, stiff and exact, and begins the count, walking the rows with the ring of keys on his belt and a tally-board in his hand. Down the room, a small boy starts to cough. Another begins to cry. Ninna's voice, pitched thin and scared, carries from near you: "He's not moving! The big one isn't moving!"

Hask stops. He looks down the row at you, grey-faced and still under your blanket, and he sighs through his nose like a man whose inventory has been damaged. The Foreman wants you alive. He comes down the row, the keys jingling, and kneels by your chained ankle with two fingers reaching for the pulse in your throat. Your Deception roll was thin, a ten, and his eyes narrow for half a heartbeat, but his hand is already coming down.

He is a pace from you, close enough to grab. The four wall-guards are at the barred door, thirty feet off, and none of them has noticed yet. You are fully rested, with Rage and your breath weapon ready, and his hand is about to touch your neck.

It is a little after six in the morning. You said you'd rage and seize him. Do you go now?

line:
I whisper back, "The goat that sings is her, Ninna, my sister the mender, so tell the little ones to be ready at her song and keep quiet till then." I ask her to have the smallest ones loosen the chute bolts' nuts if they can reach them, and to cough and moan about me at the dawn count so Hask thinks I'm dying.

Then I lie slack and gray, breathing shallow, waiting for him to come kneel by the chained prisoner the Foreman wants alive. When his hand's at my throat, I'll rage, seize him and take the key ring before he can shout.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 dawn: saw through Korvash's feigned dying (Insight nat 20). Approaches for the count with two wall-guards at his shoulders, keys on his belt, and stops out of arm's reach of the prisoner. Told Ninna's coughing is 'a poor trick'. entries.text: notebook: updated Warden Hask

In a whisper you tell Ninna that the goat who sings is your sister, the mender. Her eyes widen, then go flat and careful again. She nods, passes it down the straw in breaths and touches of the hand, and you feel it travel along the rows like a rumor. The smallest children go quiet in a way that is different from before, the quiet of waiting.

Then you lie slack and gray and breathe shallow, and the night passes. Whether it is the chain, the cold, or the body's own stubbornness, you sleep in pieces, and by the small hours the grinding ache has dulled. When the lamp gutters, you find the strength has come back into you. You have healed through the night, and the rage is a banked coal in your chest again. You keep it hidden. You keep the sagging mouth and the shallow breath.

The dawn bell tolls a little before six. Hask rises from his stool. He does the count the way he does everything, row by row, a finger lifted for each head, and Ninna coughs, loud and wet and wrong, and moans your name in a dreadful singsong. He stops. He doesn't look at her. He looks at you for a long moment, and then he says in flat Common, "A poor trick."

He doesn't kneel. He nods to the two guards behind him, and they come forward either side with shields up and longswords drawn, and stop just out of your reach. Hask stays three paces back, keys on his belt, well clear of your arms. "The Foreman said alive," he says. "He did not say whole. Lie still, Emberhide, and I will chain your other ankle, and then we will see about breakfast."

Two hobgoblins at your feet, one with the keys, two more by the door, and ninety-four children watching. You are at full strength, on the straw, chained by one ankle, and you have not yet moved.

What does Korvash do?

sheet.name: Korvash Emberhide
sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. Invent only original places and people; keep it grounded in the SRD's monsters (hobgoblins, goblins, bugbears, wolves, etc.).
